A strong outside companion is Fiona Leigh’s essay [“Self-Knowledge, Elenchus and Authority in Early Plato”](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10200368/1/Leigh%20Self-Knowledge%2C%20Elenchus%20and%20Authority%20in%20Early%20Plato%20Phrn%2020.pdf). In Chapter 5, the Caterpillar asks Alice who she is and presses her to explain herself; when she cannot, the exchange leaves her uncertainty unresolved. That makes the scene feel less like advice than an examination whose rules Alice cannot see.

Leigh’s account of Platonic *elenchus*—Socratic cross-examination—offers a useful contrast: questioning can bring cognitive self-knowledge into view, including recognition of what one does not know. The Caterpillar’s questioning can therefore be read as a distorted literary counterpart—not a straightforwardly Socratic method, but an encounter that exposes Alice’s uncertainty without giving her a stable answer.

So the connection is not that the Caterpillar is simply Socratic. It is that Chapter 5 turns philosophical questioning into a test of identity: does being asked who you are help you understand yourself, or mainly reveal how little control you have over the terms of self-definition?
